sources.headline: Italy’s Young Protesters Return to the Streets
sources.text: Fed up with the political establishment and rising cost of living, demonstrators hoped to make their message heard after violence overshadowed protests last weekend.

sources.headline: Thousands march across Italy as protests bring isolated clashes with police
sources.text:
Thousands of people took to the streets on Saturday across Italy's main cities to protest over a range of issues, including the rising cost of living, Giorgia Meloni's government and the wars in the Middle East.
The protests were mostly peaceful, although some moments of tension were reported towards the evening in Turin, Florence, Bologna and Rome.
After last weekend's violence, the government enacted a significant new security operation, with police officers and soldiers patrolling city centres.
In Milan, 500 soldiers were also deployed in response to attacks on shops last Saturday.
In Florence, as in Turin, Milan and Rome, protesters did not organise a single main march, but instead small groups gathered in different parts of the city and later joined up. They repeatedly tried to reach the city centres but were blocked by security forces.
Protesters enter the Colosseum
In Rome, tensions flared when a small group of protesters broke away from the main march on Via Cavour and headed for the Colosseum.
There, they managed to enter the Flavian Amphitheatre, chanting slogans and holding up placards. The authorities later escorted them out of the historical site as the march continued through the streets of the city.
Later on, a young demonstrator also stood in front of a police water cannon truck, which continued for a couple of metres before the young man almost ended up beneath it. Officers then forcefully dragged him away, videos circulating on social media show.
In Florence, tensions also spiked when demonstrators tried to cross the Santa Trìnita bridge, but officers maintained the security cordon and used batons as protesters pushed to break through the barrier.
In Bologna, a march was prevented from continuing towards Via Marconi and Via Reno, with bottles and other objects hurled at security forces, who responded with a water cannon and tear gas.
One person was taken to hospital after being struck by police officers.
In Milan, the situation was calmer on Saturday; at least three marches joined together and moved through the streets around the city centre. There were verbal clashes between protesters and some far-right activists.
Nine arrests made
By the end of the day, nine people had been arrested and 87 were reported to the authorities, according to the Department of Public Security. A further 371 people were taken to police stations for checks, including 110 minors and 69 foreign nationals.
In Milan, 30-year-old Youssef Siher was also detained and placed under investigation on suspicion of aggravated incitement to commit a crime. He is alleged to have been behind the "17 October Movement," a group through which thousands of people are said to have shared information about taking part in last weekend's protests.
Meloni praises security operation
In a post on social media on Saturday evening, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni praised those involved in the efforts to manage the demonstrations.
"The right to demonstrate must always be guaranteed, just as the right of citizens to live in their cities in safety," Meloni said.
"Safety must be guaranteed for everyone. For those who want to protest peacefully, for those who work and for those who want to live in their city without fear. Without leaving room for those who seek only confrontation and violence," she added.

sources.headline: Soldiers guard center of Milan as thousands of protesters march in cities across Europe
sources.text:
Members of right-wing student groups march through the streets of Rome, Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026, during a demonstration called "Unlock Everything," organized in opposition to recent left-wing student protests and one of several demonstrations held by groups across the political spectrum.
Gregorio Borgia/AP
hide caption
Gregorio Borgia/AP
MILAN — Thousands of young people marched Saturday through the streets of several Italian cities, including Milan, Rome and Turin, as authorities deployed large numbers of police and soldiers in a largely successful bid to stave off a repeat of the violent clashes and looting that marred similar protests last week.
The demonstration in Milan remained peaceful, but there were brief clashes with police in both Rome and Turin.
In Milan, thousands of young people marched the streets as soldiers were deployed and luxury boutiques were boarded up, but by late afternoon, most shops had opened, Italian media reported. Premier Giorgia Meloni announced a raft of measures, including sending an additional 500 soldiers to Milan and tougher penalties for minors, who police said made up a large part of the violent protesters last week. In Milan, police detained several minors as a preventive measure, media reported. While protests in France have claimed most international attention, large demonstrations also rocked many European cities Saturday from Milan to Rome to Madrid, Lisbon and Tirana.
Members of right-wing student groups march through the streets of Rome, Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026, during a demonstration called "Unlock Everything," organized in opposition to recent left-wing student protests and one of several demonstrations held by groups across the political spectrum.
Gregorio Borgia/AP
hide caption
Gregorio Borgia/AP
The protests encompass a broad range of issues from education and corruption to anti-war movements, pensions and housing.
Army vehicles and boarded-up luxury stores in Milan In Milan, huge crowds of mostly young people gathered as night fell, chanting insults to Meloni and holding aloft banners such as "No to lies of the state." A group of protesters dumped manure outside Italy's energy regulator and burned a symbolic, oversized electricity bill, images broadcast on local television showed. The 500 soldiers deployed to Milan came in addition to hundreds already stationed there, supporting about 5,000 police and other security personnel. Authorities used drone surveillance, checks at railway stations, rapid-response units and online monitoring for potential calls to violence. A mayoral hopeful, Pierfrancesco Majorino, who announced his candidacy Thursday, joined the marchers and remarked how peaceful the day was, according to Italian media. He will contest a center-left primary in early 2027. Milan's center-left Mayor Giuseppe Sala, who has held the role since 2016, is not running again. Many stores, particularly luxury boutiques within Milan's fashion district including Omega, Tiffany and Gucci, boarded up their front windows. The Apple store also shut down and remained shut even as others reopened.
Protesters march during a demonstration against rising living costs in Paris, Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026.
Thibault Camus/AP
hide caption
Thibault Camus/AP
Rioters last weekend smashed their way into stores, targeting sneakers, athletic wear and sporting goods on streets that run off the city's central Duomo square.
Security measures extended beyond the city center over concerns protesters could move into other neighborhoods. The protesters ended their march peacefully Saturday evening outside the Milan Polytechnic, more than 3 kilometers (2 miles) from the city center. Officials said Saturday they were investigating a 30-year-old freelance journalist said to be the "mastermind" of the newly formed Oct. 17 movement, which has been the main driver of the recent protests in Italy. Milan police say last week's violence and looting involved about 2,000 very young protesters, many of them "naturalized, second-generation Italians," alongside foreign nationals. Over two days, police arrested 45 people, including 34 minors. A group of about 30 far-right activists, described as hooligans linked to Inter Milan soccer club, made a brief appearance chanting anti-immigrant and anti-Muslim slogans but were isolated by police. Defense Minister Guido Crosetto said the soldiers deployed Saturday were only recently allowed to use plastic restraint ties and only in areas around train stations, not throughout the city. They are not authorized to carry pepper spray or tasers, he said. Protesters try to force entry into Colosseum in Rome Security was also heightened in Rome, where authorities locked down luxury shopping streets and stepped up controls around the Circus Maximus and Piazza del Popolo. A small number of protesters tried to force their way into the Colosseum, but were ushered out by guards. Elsewhere, several hundred students demonstrated peacefully to stress they were not rioters. "I think the images from last week were truly something terrible, especially for the young people, for the students, for the vast majority of the younger generations who want to study ... and do not accept being represented by those who use issues and needs to devastate entire cities," said Riccardo Ponzio, national president of an Italian far-right student association. A separate anti-war march took place in central Rome. Organizers sought to distance themselves from potential unrest, urging participants to keep their faces uncovered and hands visible.
But it was these marchers who briefly clashed with police near the Piazza della Repubblica, even as organizers were trying to hold the crowd back using batons and tear gas. In the end, the protesters pulled back when a water cannon was turned on. They retreated to a location about half a kilometer (mile) away. Clashes and buildings set on fire in Albania In Albania's capital Tirana, riot police used water cannons on large groups of protesters, some of whom set government buildings on fire and threw projectiles at police. Authorities said 2,500 officers patrolled the streets Saturday.
A protester throws a projectile towards police after a demonstration against rising living costs in Paris, Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026.
Thibault Camus/AP
hide caption
Thibault Camus/AP
For over a week, protesters have hurled rocks, flares, firebombs and fireworks at police who have used batons and tear gas in clashes in the city center. High school and university students are demanding lower tuition fees, greater state investment in education and protesting corruption in the education system. Some have joined a broader anti-government movement calling for the resignation of Socialist Prime Minister Edi Rama. A separate protest organized by the opposition outside the prime minister's office turned violent earlier, with some activists lighting fires on the street. Rama said Saturday his government was preparing a response to the students' demands and called them to a dialogue. He warned that violent protesters will face penalties. Pensions and housing spark Madrid and Lisbon protests Thousands of retirees and others marched peacefully in Spain's capital Saturday to demand public pensions aren't meddled with. "They are threatening us with privatizing pensions. It's just another thing they want to profit from," said Maria José Benito, 68. The protests came ahead of next month's snap election as Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's Socialist Party criticized the conservative opposition Popular Party for making overtures about privatizing public pensions. Spain also has been roiled by protests this fall around the issue of housing, as rental and home costs have risen in recent years beyond what many Spaniards can afford.
Taking their cue from Spaniards, protesters in Lisbon demanding affordable housing marched across the city on Saturday. They have also targeted recent measures announced by the government of Prime Minister Luis Montenegro that include easing the cap on yearly rent increases and facilitating the eviction of tenants who fail to pay rent. Montenegro defends the measures, saying that they aim at reinforcing trust between tenants and landlords and boosting the rentals market. Protesters claim that the measures are not balanced and put tenants in a more vulnerable position.

sources.headline: ‘We are suffocating’: protests spread to Lisbon and Milan as housing and living cost tensions intensify
sources.text: The angry protests that have convulsed Spain and France in recent weeks have spilled over to Italy and Portugal, with rioters clashing with police and setting property on fire in Milan, and a tent encampment springing up in Lisbon over the weekend.A march in central Milan on Saturday to protest against rising living costs began peacefully but ended with masked rioters throwing stones, paving blocks and other objects at riot police and setting fire to barricades made from bar tables.Police used water cannon and teargas to disperse the crowds, and images of the aftermath showed a severely damaged carabinieri car.Milan police clash with protesters on second day of unrestAt least two police officers were injured and about 50 demonstrators, including many minors, were detained, the LaPresse news agency reported.Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, said that while demonstrating was a right, “setting our cities ablaze is not”. In a social media post, she said “hooligans” had exploited the protests “to sow chaos, attack those responsible for ensuring security and to hold entire cities hostage”.Milan’s centre-left mayor, Giuseppe Sala, said that while “the reasons for the protests were understandable, the violence against law enforcement and serious damage to the city are not justifiable”.In Lisbon, a tent camp reminiscent of the one established in Madrid three weeks ago was set up by protesters demanding action to tackle the housing crisis and living costs.Map of protests across EuropeHundreds of protesters rallied at night in Rossio Square – located in the bustling, touristic heart of the Portuguese capital – after a march that had drawn thousands of people nationwide.The attenders vowed to stay overnight, with hundreds singing songs as they sat around the statue of King Pedro IV that dominates the square.“The Portuguese social class that pays taxes, that which keeps this country going, is under attack and is losing its rights, notably its right to housing,” said Elena Costa, a 46-year-old social assistant. “So we are all here together to try to explain that we are suffocating.”The tent camp in Rossio Square (Praça de Dom Pedro IV), Lisbon. Photograph: Manuel Fuentes/EPAAntonio Margado, a 52-year-old engineer, criticised the centre-right government for “a total liberalisation of rents; owners are protected more and more, while tenants who need a house are those who are protected less and less”.Portuguese housing prices rose by 124% between 2015 and 2024, roughly twice as fast as the EU average, according to official data. The impact is especially harsh on younger people and those in Lisbon – around a quarter of Portugal’s more than 11 million inhabitants live in the capital’s greater metropolitan area.Saturday’s camp in Lisbon amplified a housing protest that started in the northern city of Porto, where dozens of tents had already been set up.At the earlier protest in Lisbon called by the main CGTP union, demonstrators called for better public services, pensions and wages as well as measures against soaring housing costs.Protesters in Lisbon. Photograph: Filipe Amorim/AFP/Getty ImagesPortugal’s prime minister, Luís Montenegro, has said his government understood that people wanted to “express their outrage at what, in their view, may be omissions in public policies”. But he has warned political rivals against “importing into Portugal climates of instability and protest that, in fact, have no support in Portuguese society”, in a likely reference to violent protests in France.skip past newsletter promotionafter newsletter promotionThere have also been violent demonstrations in Albania this week, where demonstrators angry over university conditions and high tuition fees have demanded the resignation of the country’s prime minister, Edi Rama.On Saturday, protesters threw rocks, molotov cocktails, metal objects and pyrotechnic devices at police, and torched cars and litter bins, using them as blazing barricades to stop police advancing.In a sign of the escalating violence, police fired rubber bullets on the demonstrators for the first time since the protests began. The protests continued into the night, with buildings – including a court, banks and post office – set on fire or severely damaged.A car on fire during an anti-government demonstration outside the prime minister’s office in Tirana on Saturday. Photograph: Hameraldi Agolli/APThe unrest follows months of anti-government protests in the Balkan nation, initially sparked by a controversial resort development linked to the family of the US president, Donald Trump.Growing anger over soaring rents and social inequality boiled over in Spain last month after an 87-year-old woman was evicted from her home because she was unable to pay the 230% rent increase sought by the investment firm that had bought her flat.The plight of the late María del Carmen Abascal – and the wider issue it embodied – led to street demonstrations and the creation of a protest camp in the middle of the Spanish capital, and spurred the socialist-led government to propose emergency measures to facilitate and protect access to housing. When rightwing and far-right parties voted down those measures in congress, the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, responded by announcing a snap general election for the end of November.A banner depicting María del Carmen Abascal, reading ‘power to the people’, in Madrid on Friday. Photograph: Bernat Armangué/APIn France, fury over teacher ​absences and shabby facilities in schools in the poor northern suburbs of Paris has snowballed into a nationwide movement against inequality, weak public spending and falling standards.More than 1,200 people were arrested in France on Saturday after protesters supporting high school students clashed with police, with some demonstrations later spiralling out of control as buildings were set ablaze and shops looted.The Associated Press and Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

sources.headline: Second day of violence in Milan as protesters clash with police
Milan police clash with protesters on second day of unrest
sources.text: MILAN - Youth and police clashed for a second day on Oct 18 in Milan, where mostly black-clad assailants hurled bottles, ransacked stores, and destroyed property around the central Duomo plaza.Police in the northern city have arrested more than 200 people since Oct 17, according to Ansa news agency.Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni called for a security meeting on Oct 19 to address the violence, which resembled some scenes of chaos and looting in Paris.The Milan clashes began on Oct 17 on the sidelines of a sanctioned cost-of-living demonstration. Similar troubles took place in the northern cities of Bologna and Turin following other protests.On Oct 18, police used tear gas and water cannon to disperse groups in the Milan square, and video images showed young people, many wearing masks, throwing objects at police cars.Anti-riot police clashes with demonstrators at Piazza Duomo in Milan, on Oct 17, 2026. PHOTO: AFPA supermarket on a shopping street leading off the Duomo plaza was ransacked, garbage cans overturned and scooters and bicycles vandalised.The mayor of Milan, Giuseppe Sala, said that he had witnessed “smashed shop windows, looted stores, and frightened citizens”.“What happened here is what we are seeing in many cities around the world,” he told Ansa.“I’m very worried because it’s a new phenomenon, which also originates from an international scenario and therefore feeds itself.”Far-right prime minister Meloni on Oct 17 called the vandals “thugs who exploit demonstrations to spread chaos, attack those who guarantee security, and hold entire cities hostage”.“To demonstrate is a right. To lay our cities to waste is not,” she wrote on X. AFP
